newsitem.title: USA: Lifestyle may play role in breast implant disease.
newsitem.headline: Lifestyle may play role in breast implant disease.

text.p: Women who undergo breast implant surgery tend to be heavier drinkers and have more sex partners, lifestyle choices that may be a factor in illnesses blamed on their implants, a study released on Tuesday said.

Research on 3,750 women found that those with implants were nearly three times more likely to have seven or more alcoholic drinks per week, about 4.5 times more likely to have used hair dyes and nearly nine times as likely to have had at least 14 sexual partners.

"We found that some demographic, lifestyle, reproductive and medical characteristics of women with breast augmentation were notably different than those among women in general in our sample population," Linda Cook of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Centre in Seattle wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
The team said the differences, which also included the number of pregnancies and use of oral contraceptives, were important "insofar as they influence the risk of a given disease."

Silicone-filled implants have been linked to auto-immune diseases and other problems, although the majority of epidemiologic studies done to date have found little, if any, adverse health effects from implants.
The Seattle researchers said their study highlighted the need to factor in lifestyle characteristics that may have contributed to an illness blamed on implants.

Deborah del Junco of the Veterans Affairs Medical Centre in Houston wrote in an accompanying editorial that the study will give other researchers the advantage of being able to evaluate a number of potentially important disease risk factors. The research "brings us back, full circle, to the original question of the long-term health risks associated with breast implant surgery," del Junco said.
"Only this time, we are asked to consider alternative explanations for the association -- or lack of association, as the case may be -- between breast implants and the disease outcomes of interest."
